(Surah al-Falaq) Five verses, Medinan.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak.﴾

﴿Bismillah﴾

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak.﴾ On it there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Regarding His saying "Say" (qul), there are several benefits.

First: When He, glory be to Him, commanded the recitation of Surat al-Ikhlas, which declares Him free of what does not befit His essence and attributes, and this is among the greatest acts of worship, it is as if the servant said: "O our God, this act of worship is very great; I do not trust myself to fulfill it." So He answered by saying: ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾, that is, seek refuge in Allah and turn to Him, so that He may enable you to perform this act of worship in the most complete manner.

Second: When the disbelievers asked the Messenger about the lineage and description of Allah, it is as if the Messenger, peace be upon him, said: "How shall I be saved from these ignorant people who dared to say about You what does not befit You?" So Allah said: ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾, that is, seek refuge in Me, so that I may protect you from their evil.

Third: It is as if He, exalted, says: "Whoever takes refuge in My House, I honor him and make him safe. I have said: whoever enters it is safe. So take refuge in Me as well, so that I may make you safe": so ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾.

**The second issue:** Scholars have differed on whether it is permissible to seek help through incantations (ruqa) and charms (ʿawadh). Some said it is permissible, and they argued with several points:

First: It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) fell ill, and Jibril (peace be upon him) recited over him, saying: "In the name of Allah I recite over you from everything that harms you; may Allah cure you."

Second: Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to teach us, for all pains and fever, this supplication: In the name of Allah, the Generous; I seek refuge in Allah, the Mighty, from the evil of every throbbing vein, and from the evil of the heat of the Fire."

Third: He, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever visits a sick person whose time of death has not come, and says: I ask Allah, the Mighty, Lord of the Mighty Throne, to cure you seven times, he will be cured."

Fourth: Ali (peace be upon him) said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) visited a sick person, he would say: Remove the affliction, O Lord of mankind; cure, You are the Healer; there is no healer but You."

Fifth: From Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to seek protection for al-Hasan and al-Husayn, saying: I place you under the protection of the perfect words of Allah from every devil and vermin, and from every envious evil eye. And he would say: Thus my father Ibrahim used to seek protection for his two sons, Ismaʿil and Ishaq."

Sixth: ʿUthman ibn Abi al-ʿAs al-Thaqafi said: "I came to the Messenger of Allah while I had a pain that had nearly destroyed me. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: Place your right hand upon it and say: In the name of Allah, I seek refuge in the might and power of Allah from the evil of what I feel, seven times. I did that, and Allah cured me."

Seventh: It is narrated that when he, peace be upon him, travelled and stopped at a place, he would say: O earth, my Lord and your Lord is Allah. I seek refuge in Allah from your evil, the evil of what is in you, the evil of what emerges from you, and the evil of what crawls upon you. And I seek refuge in Allah from lions, lion-kind, serpents and scorpions, and from the evil of the inhabitants of the land, and of the begetter and what he begot.

Eighth: ʿAʾisha said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) complained of any pain in his body, he would recite Surat al-Ikhlas, ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 1], and the two protective surahs (al-Muʿawwidhatayn), into his right palm, and wipe with it the place where he felt pain."

Some people prohibited incantations, relying on what is narrated from Jabir: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade incantations," and he, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed, there are servants of Allah who do not seek cauterization nor ask for incantation, and upon their Lord they rely."

He, peace be upon him, also said: "He who seeks cauterization and asks for incantation has not relied upon Allah." It has been answered that the prohibition may refer to unknown incantations whose realities are not known; as for what has a reliable basis, there is no prohibition against it.

They differed regarding amulets (taʿlil). It is narrated that he, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever hangs something (as protection) will be left to it." And from Ibn Masʿud: he saw on the arm of his concubine (umm walad) an amulet tied to her upper arm, so he pulled it violently and broke it.

Among them, some permitted it. Al-Baqir (peace be upon him) was asked about a charm hung on children, and he permitted it.

They also differed about spitting (nafth). It is narrated from ʿAʾisha that she said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was ill, he would blow upon himself with the protective surahs and wipe with his hands. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) became ill with the illness from which he died, I began to blow upon him with the protective surahs with which he used to blow upon himself."

And from him, peace be upon him: "When he lay down on his bed, he would blow into his hands and recite the protective surahs over them, then wipe his body with them."

Among them, some denied spitting. ʿIkrima said: "It is not proper for the one who recites over a sick person to spit, to wipe, or to tie knots." And from Ibrahim: "They used to dislike spitting in incantations." Some of them said: "I entered upon al-Dahhak while he was in pain, and I said: Shall I recite over you, O Abu Muhammad? He said: Yes, but do not spit. So I recited over him with the two protective surahs."

Al-Halimi said: What is narrated from ʿIkrima, that the one who recites should not spit, wipe, or tie knots, seems to have been based on the view that Allah made spitting into knots among the things one seeks refuge from, so it must be forbidden. But this is weak, because spitting into knots is only blameworthy when it is sorcery harmful to souls and bodies; as for when this spitting is for the healing of souls and bodies, it must not be unlawful.

* * *

**The third issue:** He, exalted, said at the opening of the recitation: ﴿So seek refuge in Allah﴾, and here He said: ﴿I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾, and in another place: ﴿And say: My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the whisperings of the devils﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 97]. And in the hadiths comes: "I seek refuge in the perfect words of Allah." There is no doubt that the best of Allah's names is Allah, while "Lord" (Rabb) may be applied to others, as He said: ﴿Are lords dispersed (better), or Allah, the One, the Irresistible?﴾ [Yusuf: 39]. So what is the reason that, when commanding seeking refuge, He did not say "I seek refuge in Allah," but said: ﴿in the Lord of the daybreak﴾? They answered in several ways:

First: In His saying: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah﴾ [al-Nahl: 98], He commanded seeking refuge there for the sake of reciting the Qur'an, while here, in this surah, He commanded seeking refuge for the protection of the self and body from sorcery. The first matter is more important, so the Greatest Name was rightly mentioned there.

Second: The devil exerts far greater effort to prevent you from worship than to harm your body and soul. Therefore the Greatest Name was mentioned there, not here.

Third: The name "Lord" (Rabb) points to nurture (tarbiyah). It is as if He made His nurturing of you in the past a means to His nurturing of you in the future. Or the servant says: "Nurturing and beneficence are Your craft, so do not neglect me, and do not disappoint my hope."

Fourth: By nurturing, one becomes a beginner in beneficence, and beginning obliges completion.

Fifth: This surah is the last of the surahs of the Qur'an, so He mentioned the word "Lord" to alert that His nurturing and beneficence never cease for you. If it is said: He concluded the Qur'an with the name "God" where He said: ﴿The King of mankind, the God of mankind﴾ [al-Nas: 2–3], we say: there is a subtle point in it, which is that He, exalted, said: "Say: I seek refuge in the One who is my Lord; yet He is a God who subdues the whisperer who slinks away." He is like a compassionate father, so that you say: "Return in your great affairs to your father who is compassionate towards you, who is like a sharp sword and a burning fire against your enemies." This is among the greatest kinds of promise of beneficence and nurturing.

Sixth: It is as if the Truth said to Muhammad (peace be upon him): "Your heart is for Me, so do not let love of other than Me enter it; your tongue is for Me, so do not mention anyone else with it; your body is for Me, so do not occupy it with serving other than Me. If you want something, do not ask for it except from Me. If you want knowledge, say: ﴿My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾ [Ta-Ha: 114]; if you want the world, ask Allah of His bounty; and if you fear harm, say: ﴿I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾. For I am the One who described Myself as the Creator of the dawn, and the Splitter of the grain and the date-stone. I did not do these things except for your sake. So when I do all these things for your sake, shall I not protect you from calamities and fears?"

* * *

**The fourth issue:** They mentioned several meanings of "al-falaq" (daybreak):

First: It is the dawn, which is the view of most scholars. Al-Zajjaj said: because the dawn is split and cleft from the night. It is a form (faʿal) in the sense of a passive participle (mafʿul). One says: "He is clearer than the falaq of the dawn," and "than the faraq of the dawn." Its specification in seeking refuge is for several reasons:

The first: The One who is able to remove these intense darknesses from this whole world is also able to repel from the one seeking refuge everything he fears and dreads.

The second: The rising of dawn is like an example of the coming of relief. Just as a person at night awaits the morning, so the frightened person awaits the dawn of success.

The third: The dawn is like good tidings, for a person in darkness is like flesh upon a wooden board. When dawn appears, it is as if it calls out safety and announces relief. For this reason every sick and anxious person finds ease at the time of pre-dawn. So the Truth, glory be to Him, says: "Say: I seek refuge in a Lord who bestows the blessing of the splitting of dawn before the request; how much more after the request."

The fourth: Some said: when Yusuf (peace be upon him) was thrown into the well, his knee was struck with severe pain, so he spent the night awake. When the dawn drew near, Jibril (peace be upon him) descended by Allah's leave to console him and command him to supplicate his Lord. He said: "O Jibril, you supplicate and I will say Amen." Jibril supplicated and Yusuf said Amen, so Allah removed the harm he had. When Yusuf's time came, Jibril said: "I will supplicate too, and you say Amen." So Yusuf asked his Lord to remove the harm from all the people of affliction at that time. Therefore every sick person finds some kind of relief in the last part of the night. It is narrated that his supplication in the well was: "O my support in my hardship, O my companion in my loneliness, O my compassionate one in my exile, O remover of my distress, O answerer of my call, O my God and the God of my fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, have mercy on my young age, my weak support, and my lack of means. O Living, O Self-Subsisting, O Possessor of Majesty and Honor."

The fifth: Perhaps the specification of the dawn in mention in this place is because it is the time when the distressed supplicate and the afflicted are answered. It is as if He says: "Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the time when every anxious person is relieved."

The sixth: It may be that He specified the dawn for mention because it is a model of the Day of Resurrection. Creation is like the dead, and homes are like graves. Then some of them come out of their houses bankrupt and naked, unheeded; some were indebted and are dragged to prison; some were kings obeyed, before whom mounts are brought and people stand before them. Likewise on the Day of Resurrection: some are bankrupt of reward, naked of the garment of piety, dragged before the Mighty King; and whoever worshipped and was obedient to his Lord in this world becomes a obeyed king in the next, to whom the Buraq is brought.

The seventh: It may be that He, exalted, specified the dawn for mention because it is the time of the congregational prayer which gathers the states of the Resurrection. Standing in prayer reminds one of standing on the Day of Resurrection, as He said: ﴿The Day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 6]. Recitation in prayer reminds one of the reading of the books. Bowing in prayer reminds one of His saying: ﴿with their heads bowed﴾ [al-Sajdah: 12]. Prostration in prayer reminds one of His saying: ﴿and they are called to prostrate, but they will not be able﴾ [al-Qalam: 42]. Sitting reminds one of His saying: ﴿and you will see every nation kneeling﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 28]. So the servant says: "My God, as You delivered me from the darkness of the night, deliver me from these terrors." The time of the dawn prayer was specified because it has greater honor, as He said: ﴿Indeed, the recitation of dawn is witnessed﴾ [al-Isra: 78], that is, the angels of the night and the day attend it.

The eighth: it is the time of seeking forgiveness and supplication, as He said: ﴿and those who seek forgiveness at dawn﴾ [Al 'Imran: 17].

The second opinion regarding *al-falaq* (the daybreak) is that it is an expression for everything that God splits: the earth for plants, as in ﴿Indeed, God is the splitter of the grain and the date-stone﴾ [al-An'am: 95]; mountains for springs; indeed, among stones are those from which rivers gush forth; clouds for rain; wombs for children; eggs for chicks; and hearts for knowledge. If you reflect upon creation, it becomes clear to you that most of it is through transformation. Rather, non-existence is like darkness, and existence is like light. It is established that God was in eternity and nothing whatsoever was with Him. So it is as if He, glorified is He, is the One who split the seas of the darkness of non-existence with the lights of bringing into being, fashioning and originating. This is what is meant by *al-falaq*. This interpretation is closer to the truth than other possibilities, for several reasons:

First: the existent is either the Creator or the created. When we interpret *al-falaq* in this way, it is as if He said: Say, "I seek refuge in the Lord of all possible things, and the Maker of all originated and innovated things." Thus the glorification in it is greater, and the dawn is one of the matters included in this meaning.

Second: every existent is either necessary in its essence or possible in its essence. The possible in its essence is existent through another and non-existent in itself. Therefore every possible thing necessarily has an influencer that acts upon it at the time of its coming into being and sustains it at the time of its continuance, for the possible thing in its continuance also needs an influencer. *At-tarbiyah* (nurturing) is an indication not only of the state of coming into being but of the state of continuance. It is as if He says: "You are not in need only at the time of coming into being; rather, at the time of coming into being and at the time of continuance together, both in essence and in all attributes." So His saying ﴿Lord of the daybreak﴾ indicates that everything other than Him needs Him in both states, coming into being and continuance, in quiddity and existence, according to essences and attributes. The secret of tawhid (monotheism) is not purified of the taints of shirk (associating partners with God) except upon witnessing these meanings.

Third: depicting and forming in darkness is more difficult than in light. It is as if He says: "I am the One who does what He does before the rising of lights and the appearance of illuminations, and such things that cannot be achieved except with perfect knowledge and consummate wisdom." To this points His saying: ﴿He it is who forms you in the wombs as He wills. There is no god but He, the Mighty, the Wise﴾ [Al 'Imran: 6].

The third opinion: it is a valley in Hell, or a pit in it, from their saying about what has settled into the ground: *falaq*, and its plural is *fulqan*. It is narrated from one of the Companions that he came to Syria and saw the houses of the *ahl al-dhimma* (protected non-Muslim subjects) and the abundance of comfortable living they were in. He said, "I am not concerned. Is there not behind them the *falaq*?" It was asked, "What is the *falaq*?" He said, "A house in Hell; when it is opened, all the people of the Fire cry out because of the intensity of its heat." He singled it out for mention here because He is the One capable of such a great punishment, beyond the imaginings of creatures. Then it is established that His mercy is greater, more complete and more perfect than His punishment. So it is as if he says: "O Possessor of severe punishment, I seek refuge in Your mercy, which is greater, more complete, more perfect, earlier and more ancient than Your punishment."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿From the evil of what He created﴾. In this there are two issues.

The first issue: concerning the interpretation of this verse, there are several views.

The first: ʿAṭāʾ reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that it refers specifically to Iblis, because God Most High has not created any creature more evil than him. Also, the surah was revealed concerning seeking refuge from magic, and that is only accomplished through Iblis and his helpers and soldiers.

The second: it refers to Hell (Jahannam), as if He is saying: Say, "I seek refuge in the Lord of Hell, and from the severe things He created therein."

The third: ﴿from the evil of what He created﴾ means from the evil of the kinds of harmful animals, such as predators, venomous creatures, and others. It is also permissible that it includes those among the jinn and humans who harm me. He described their actions as evil. The inclusion of jinn and humans under the word "mā" is permissible because, when the majority of reference was to non-rational beings, it is good to use the word "mā" for them as well, since the consideration is given to the majority. It also includes the harms of foods that cause illness, and the harms of water and fire. If it is said: the pains that follow from water and fire, and the sting of a snake or scorpion, occur by God's creation directly according to the view of most of the mutakallimun (theologians), or they arise from powers that God Most High created in these bodies, according to the view of the majority of the ḥukamāʾ (philosophers) and some of the mutakallimun, then in either case the meaning of the verse becomes that He commanded the Messenger, upon him be peace, to seek refuge in God from God. What is its meaning? We say: and what harm is there in that? He, upon him be peace, indeed stated this explicitly when he said: "And I seek refuge in You from You."

The fourth: He meant by it what He created of diseases, illnesses, drought, various trials and calamities. Al-Jubbāʾī and al-Qadi claimed that this interpretation is false, because the act of God Most High cannot be described as evil. They said: several points prove this:

The first: on this interpretation it would follow that the One from whom He commanded us to seek refuge is the One whom He commanded us to seek refuge in, and that is contradictory.

The second: all the acts of God are wisdom and rightness, and that does not permit saying that it is evil.

The third: if the act of God were evil, its Doer would be described as wicked, and God is exalted above that.

The answer to the first: We have shown that there is no impossibility in the saying "I seek refuge in You from You."

The answer to the second: when a person suffers from it, it is regarded as evil, so the wording came in accordance with that statement, as in His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40], and His saying: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same way as he transgressed against you﴾ [al-Baqara: 194].

The answer to the third: the names of God are based on revelation (tawqīfiyya), not on convention (iṣṭilāḥiyya). Then, what indicates the permissibility of calling diseases and illnesses "evils" is His saying: ﴿When evil touches him, he is distressed﴾ [al-Maʿarij: 20], and His saying: ﴿And when evil touches him, he is one of lengthy supplication﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 51]. The Prophet, upon him be peace, used to say: "And I seek refuge in You from the evil of the nightly and daytime visitors."

The second issue: some of the heretics (mulḥida) objected to His saying: ﴿Say, "I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak" ﴿from the evil of what He created﴾ from several angles:

The first: is the thing sought refuge from happening by the decree and predestination of God, or not by His decree and not by His predestination? If it is the first, how is he commanded to seek refuge in God from it? That is because whatever God has decreed and predestined will certainly occur. So it is as if He is saying: "The thing I have decreed to occur, and which must occur, so seek refuge in Me from it, so that I do not bring it about." And if it is not by His decree and predestination, then that impugns the dominion of God and His sovereignty.

The second: if what is sought refuge from is known to occur, then there is no preventer of it, so there is no benefit in seeking refuge; and if it is known to occur, there is no need for seeking refuge.

The third: if what is sought refuge from is a benefit, how is the responsible person eager to seek its removal and prevention? And if it is a harm, how did He create and predestine it? Know that the answer to such doubts is to say that He "cannot be questioned about what He does" (﴿لا يُسْألُ عَمّا يَفْعَلُ﴾, al-Anbiya: 23), and this statement has been repeated in this book.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And from the evil of darkness when it settles﴾. The commentators have mentioned several meanings for *al-ghasiq* (the darkness):

First: *al-ghasiq* is the night when its darkness becomes intense, from His saying: ﴿until the darkness of the night﴾. From this comes *ghasaqat al-'ayn* (the eye became full of tears) when it fills with tears, and *ghasaqat al-jarahah* (the wound became full) when it fills with blood. This is the view of al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayda. Ibn Qays recited:

"Indeed this night has grown dark, and I have complained of worry and sleeplessness."

al-Zajjaj said: *al-ghasiq* in the language means the cold, and the night was called *ghasiq* because it is colder than the day. From this comes His saying: "It is the *zamharir*" (the intense cold).

Third: some people said: *al-ghasiq* and *al-ghassaq* mean the flowing one, from their saying: *ghasaqat al-'ayn yaghsiqu ghasqan* when the eye flowed with water. The night was called *ghasiq* because its darkness pours down upon the earth. As for *al-wuqub*, it is entering into something in such a way that it disappears from the eye. One says: *waqaba yaqibu wuquban* when he entered. *Al-waqbah* is a hollow, because water enters it. *Al-iqab* is putting a thing into a *waqbah*. This is what relates to the language. As for the commentators on the verse, they have several sayings:

First: *al-ghasiq* when it settles is the night when it enters. He only commanded seeking refuge from the evil of the night because in the night wild beasts come out of their thickets and vermin out of their places, the thief and the assailant attack, fire breaks out, and help is scarce. For this reason, if an aggressor (*mu'tadin*) draws a weapon against a person at night and kills him, the one who was attacked does not incur *qisas* (retaliation), whereas if it were by day he would incur it, because help is available then. Some people said: at night harmful spirits called jinn and devils spread out, because the strength of the sun's rays seems to overpower them, whereas at night they gain a kind of control.

Second: *al-ghasiq* when it settles is the moon. Ibn Qutaybah said: *al-ghasiq* is the moon, so called because it is eclipsed and thus *yughsaq*, meaning its light goes away and it turns black, and its *wuqub* is its entering into that blackening. Abu Salamah narrated from 'A'ishah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took her hand, pointed to the moon, and said: "Seek refuge in Allah from the evil of this, for it is the *ghasiq* when it settles." Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning of his saying "seek refuge in Allah from its evil when it settles" is when it enters the eclipse. In my view there is another aspect: it is established that the moon in its body is not luminous but dark, and this is the intended meaning of its being *ghasiq*. As for its *wuqub*, it is the effacement of its light at the end of the month. The astrologers say that at the end of the month it is inauspicious and weak in power, because its light continues to diminish, and because of this its ill-omen increases. For this reason sorcerers only busy themselves with the kind of magic that causes illness at this time. This suits the occasion of the revelation of the surah, for it was revealed only because they had bewitched the Prophet (ﷺ) so as to make him ill.

Third: Ibn Zayd said: *al-ghasiq* when it settles means the Pleiades (*al-Thurayya*) when it sets, he said. Illnesses used to increase at its setting and decrease at its rising. On this view the Pleiades is called *ghasiq* because it pours down when it sets in the west, and its *wuqub* is its entering beneath the earth and its disappearance from sight.

Fourth: the author of *al-Kashshaf* said: it is permissible that *al-ghasiq* means the black snake, and its *wuqub* is its striking and piercing, and *al-wuqb* and *al-naqb* are the same. Know that this interpretation is the weakest of the mentioned views.

Fifth: *al-ghasiq* when it settles is the sun when it sets. It was called *ghasiq* because it moves in the sphere, so its motion and course were named *al-ghasaq*. Its *wuqub* is its disappearance and its entering beneath the earth.

**Commentary on His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿And from the evil of those who blow in knots﴾. In this verse there are several issues:**

**The first issue: concerning the verse there are two opinions.**

**The first:** *al-nafth* (blowing) is blowing accompanied by saliva. This is what the author of *al-Kashshaf* (Al-Zamakhshari's exegesis) said. Others among them say it is blowing alone, and from it is His peace be upon him saying: "Indeed Jibril blew (*nafatha*) into my heart." *Al-'uqad* is the plural of *'uqdah* (knot). The reason for this is that when the sorcerer begins to recite the incantation (*ruqyah*), he takes a thread and keeps tying knot after knot upon it, blowing into those knots. He used the feminine form *al-naffathat* (those who blow) for several reasons:

- **The first:** This craft is known to be practised by women, because they tie knots and blow. This is because its greatest foundation is binding the heart to that matter and firmly focusing the aspiration and imagination upon it. This comes more readily from women, owing to their lesser knowledge and their greater desire. Therefore this action is stronger when they do it. Abu 'Ubaydah said: *al-naffathat* are the daughters of Labid ibn A'sam, the Jew, who bewitched the Prophet (ﷺ).

- **The second:** What is meant by *al-naffathat* is the souls (*nufus*).

- **The third:** What is meant by them is groups, because whenever more sorcerers gather for a single action, the effect is stronger.

**The second opinion**, which is the choice of Abu Muslim (al-Isfahani), is: ﴿And from the evil of those who blow in knots﴾, meaning women, "in the knots", meaning in men's resolutions and opinions. It is a metaphor taken from the tying of ropes. *Al-nafth* is softening a knot in a rope by casting saliva upon it so that its untying becomes easy. So the meaning of the verse is that women, because of the abundance of their love in men's hearts, manipulate men, turning them from one opinion to another and from one resolve to another. Therefore God commanded His Messenger to seek refuge from their evil, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, among your spouses and your children there are enemies to you, so beware of them﴾ [al-Taghabun: 14]. For this reason God magnified their scheming, saying: ﴿Indeed, your scheming is great﴾ [Yusuf: 28].

Know that this opinion is good, were it not that it contradicts the view of most of the exegetes (*mufassirun*).

**The third issue:** The Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school) denied that magic has any real effect, and this issue has already been discussed. Then they said: the reason for seeking refuge from their evil is in three respects:

- **The first:** that one seeks refuge from the sin of their practice of magic.
- **The second:** that one seeks refuge from their tempting people through their magic.
- **The third:** that one seeks refuge from their feeding people bad foods that cause madness and death.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 113, verse 5:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And from the evil of an envier when he envies﴾. It is known that the envier is one whose desire to remove the blessing of another from them is intense, and he is hardly like this unless, if he were able to do so by stratagems, he would do it. Therefore Allah commanded seeking refuge from him. Every evil that is guarded against and protected from, in religion and in worldly life, has entered into this surah. Therefore, when it was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rejoiced at its revelation, because it, together with what follows it, comprises seeking refuge against every matter. It is also permissible that by the evil of the envier is meant his sin and the ugliness of his state at the time of his envy and the manifestation of its effect.

Two questions remain here:

The first question: His saying, ﴿From the evil of what He created﴾, is general in respect of everything from which refuge is sought, so what is the meaning of seeking refuge after it from the darkness when it gathers (al-ghasiq), the blowers in knots (al-naffathat), and the envier?

The answer: To draw attention to the fact that these evils are the greatest kinds of evil.

The second question: Why did He define some of what is sought refuge from and indefinite some of it?

The answer: He defined the blowers (al-naffathat), because every blower in knots is evil. And He made ghasiq indefinite, because not every darkness is evil. Likewise, not every envier is evil; rather, there is envy that is praiseworthy, and that is envy in good things.

And Allah, glorified and exalted, knows best, and may Allah's blessings be upon our master Muhammad, and upon his family and companions, and grant them peace.
